item.title: ‘Crazy Vainī’ lives up to its name as supporters block the police escort and team bus to keep Tonga’s rugby heroes a little longer

item.content:encoded:
Tonga’s national rugby league team received an extraordinary homecoming welcome in Vaini, where supporters brought a police-escorted convoy to a halt after a van was parked in the middle of the road, with its driver and keys nowhere to be found.

The roadblock was part of a worldwide expression of the māfana and fakavelevela spirit of Tongan supporters, whose unwavering passion for their national team remained undiminished despite its 34–10 semi-final defeat to the New Zealand Kiwis, which ended Tonga’s hopes of reaching the World Cup final.

The incident, captured on camera in footage seen by Kaniva News, unfolded as police escorted the returning players from Fuaʻamotu International Airport.

The footage showed what appeared to be police officers, unable to remove the vehicle, manoeuvring their van around the roadblock. However, the bus carrying the team remained blocked.

It was unclear whether the driver was eventually located or how the situation was resolved.

The convoy was heading to Nukuʻalofa, about 35 kilometres away, with plans to slow down or make brief stops along the way to allow players to greet and celebrate with residents and supporters.

The roadblock was reportedly intentional, allowing supporters to spend more time with their sporting heroes while police attempted to remove the vehicle.

Footage showed crowds dressed in Tonga’s national colours of red and white, waving flags and celebrating alongside police vehicles.

The incident appeared to live up to the town’s colourful nickname, “Vaini Vale”, literally meaning “Crazy Vaini”, a name coined in recognition of its residents’ unconventional, exuberant and sometimes mischievous behaviour.

The Vainī homecoming was one of several stops along Taufaʻāhau Road from Fuaʻamotu, including Veitongo and Havelu, where players paused to greet cheering supporters and briefly mingle with residents before continuing to Nukuʻalofa.

The celebrations followed weeks of passionate displays of support for Tonga National Rugby League XIII, uniting Tongan communities across the globe.

In New Zealand and Australia, supporters organised vehicle convoys, flag parades and community gatherings throughout the tournament.

Similar celebrations took place in Portland, Utah and Hawaii in the United States, where members of the Tongan diaspora rallied behind the team.

In Tonga, the festivities extended beyond Tongatapu. In Vavaʻu, social media influencer Siaki Lonitenisi organised a colourful bicycle parade involving children and adults, while supporters in ʻEua staged their own red-and-white procession.

Despite the disappointment of missing out on the final, fans took to social media to express their pride in the team, posting messages such as “Go Mate Maʻa Tonga! Win or lose, we still support you!”

The scenes in Vaini reflected that enduring loyalty, as Tonga’s players returned home to a welcome more commonly associated with champions.
